(a) In General.—Subsection (b) of section 179 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (relating to limitations) is amended by adding at the end the following new paragraph:“(7) Increase in limitations for 2008.—In the case of any taxable year beginning in 2008—“(A) the dollar limitation under paragraph (1) shall be $250,000,“(B) the dollar limitation under paragraph (2) shall be $800,000, and“(C) the amounts described in subparagraphs (A) and (B) shall not be adjusted under paragraph (5).”. 
    (b) Effective Date.—The amendment made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2007.

fable.w: This section only amends section 179 of the Internal Revenue Code to raise the expensing dollar limitations for taxable years beginning in 2008 and sets an effective date. No tempting reading really arises: it involves no rulemaking, comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue. No party outside the federal government takes part in any federal decision.

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to set specific dollar limitations for tax deductions. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government. The text is purely substantive legislation regarding tax limits, with no procedural requirements for public input or external advisory bodies.
qwen_block.s: (a) In General.—Subsection (b) of section 179 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (relating to limitations) is amended by adding at the end the following new paragraph:“(7) Increase in limitations for 2008.—In the case of any taxable year beginning in 2008—“(A) the dollar limitation under paragraph (1) shall be $250,000,“(B) the dollar limitation under paragraph (2) shall be $800,000, and“(C) the amounts described in subparagraphs (A) and (B) shall not be adjusted under paragraph (5).”.

opus.w: This section only changes the dollar limits on the section 179 expensing deduction for 2008 and sets when the change takes effect. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue. It also gives no agency authority to issue regulations, so it does not count as rulemaking participation. The only tempting reading would treat any change to the tax code as a decision affecting the public, but the section never asks anyone outside the federal government for input.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to set specific dollar limitations for tax deductions and establishes an effective date. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or experts) before the decision is made. The changes are legislative mandates, not procedural requirements for agency decision-making involving external stakeholders.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing tax limitations affects the public, so it involves participation. However, the definition requires that the government *consult or coordinate* with outsiders *before* making a decision. This section simply sets statutory numbers and effective dates; it does not establish a process for public input, advisory committees, or consultation with states or tribes. The "decision" here is made by Congress through legislation, not by an agency consulting with outsiders.
